before: A property pattern inspects a member without changing it. In { Score: >= 5 }, Score names the property and >= 5 tests its value. The pattern does not match null.
A switch expression tests its arms in order and chooses the first match. => separates a pattern from its result; _ is the fallback pattern. The final semicolon ends the assignment.
The relational pattern >= includes equality. A lower score takes the fallback in this two-arm example. The result string is a label, not a change to the record.
Expected behavior from this example: Ready. This expected result is a reasoned prediction until a compiler test is recorded.

Optional local transfer task: Test scores 4, 5, 6 and add a higher first arm for scores at least 10; explain why arm order matters. Use a .NET 10 console project with C# 14; reading completion does not verify this local work.
after: A pattern describes a condition a value must match. This switch uses a pattern to decide which label fits a study result.
{ Score: >= 5 } checks that the object exists and its Score is at least five. The colon names the property to check; it does not assign a new score.
The switch checks its choices in order. The first matching pattern supplies its result after =>. The final _ handles anything left over.
The program prints Ready because 6 is at least 5. A score of exactly 5 also matches because >= includes equality.
The switch reads the score and returns text. It does not raise or lower the stored score. A missing object would not match the property pattern.
